title: Two Practical Reminder Strategies for Overcoming Noise-Induced Aimlessness
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This is the follow-up to Stuart's piece on noise, and it converts the diagnosis into two concrete reminder practices for educators. He opens with the film Memento, whose protagonist tattoos his purpose onto his body, and inverts it: teachers remember the latest distraction and forget their abiding purpose. Citing Kathleen Eisenhardt and Donald Sull on simple rules, he insists that complex problems do not require complex solutions. The first practice comes from Chris Lowney's account of Pope Francis, who wrote a personal credo of under two hundred words before ordination and has revisited it for decades; Stuart asks readers to write and periodically edit their own. The second is his own hand-lettered chart paper carrying his Everest statement, posted publicly in the classroom so that students and colleagues become part of the reminder system. The rhetorical move in the middle is a direct challenge to teacher self-pity: if a man responsible for over a billion Catholics under constant media scrutiny can hold his purpose, a teacher's excuses do not hold. The piece closes by urging readers to build the reminder in January, when they are at their best, precisely because February and May will find them at their worst.
points: Stuart's structural claim is that our aimlessness is externally initiated, internally located and practically solvable, which is why the fix is a physical reminder rather than more willpower.
The Pope Francis credo exercise gives a usable specification: under two hundred words, deeply personal and concrete, revisited and edited rather than filed away.
He argues for posting the Everest statement publicly in the classroom or staff lounge instead of taping it to a monitor, so colleagues and students share the job of reminding you.
The piece insists that solutions to complex problems should stay simple, borrowing from Simple Rules that complicated answers to complex problems usually add confusion.
The timing advice is the memorable move: build the reminder during the month you are at your best so it survives the months when you are at your worst.
quotes: When I look at my students and I look at myself, I see that we have something in common: we are all pretty much the opposite of Leonard. We lose sight of our single, abiding purposes and instead keep in mind only the latest short-term memories — our Twitter or Facebook streams; the book we're reading right now; the most recent show we've binge-watched or podcast we've heard.

His problem was externally initiated (he got hit in the head), internally located (his condition), and practically solved (his reminder system). Our problem is externally initiated (more choices, or noise , than ever before in human history), internally located (we form habits around our favorite sources of noise), and practically solved.

First, in line with the above quoted Simple Rules , the solutions to our noise-induced aimlessness need not be complex. Francis, in an inspired moment, wrote a less-than-200-word personal credo. Later in the passage, we learn that he cultivated the habit of regularly reflecting on that credo and whether he was living it out (or whether it needed editing).

Second, if the pope can keep in mind who he is and what his purpose is despite the pressures of his job, then we can, too. If you think the pope has an easier time remaining true to his purpose than today's American public school teacher, you're not thinking clearly.

I've heard of some folks who take their Everest statement and put it on an index card and tape it to their computer monitors. But perhaps there's a benefit in sharing it with others — in the staff lounge, or (as in my example) in the front of our classrooms. This way, it's not just the reminder that can remind us of our abiding purposes in our work — our students or our colleagues can help, too.

I heard it said recently that when we're at our best we ought to prepare for when we're at our worst. January, the month of resolutions and life-changey things , is often a month in which we're at our best. Before the month ends, schedule the time to create something — a Francis-esque credo, a Stuart-esque hand-scrawled chart paper — to remind Future You what in the world it was that you set out to do when the tougher months of February or May come along this year.
